'''Alexis Claude Clairaut''' ({{IPAc-en|k|l|ɛə|ˈ|r|oʊ}};<ref>{{Cite Dictionary.com|Clairaut}}</ref> {{IPA|fr|alɛksi klod klɛʁo|lang}}; 13 May 1713 – 17 May 1765) was a French mathematician, [[astronomer]], and physicist. He was a prominent Newtonian whose work helped to establish the validity of the principles and results that Sir [[Isaac Newton]] had outlined in the ''[[Principia Mathematica Philosophiae Naturalis|Principia]]'' of 1687. Clairaut was one of the key figures in the expedition to the [[Sápmi|Lapland]] that helped to confirm Newton's deduction of the [[figure of the Earth]]. In that context, Clairaut deduced what is now known as [[Clairaut's theorem (gravity)|Clairaut's theorem]]. He also tackled the gravitational [[three-body problem]], being the first to obtain a satisfactory result for the [[apsidal precession]] of the Moon's orbit. In mathematics he is also credited with [[Symmetry of second derivatives|Clairaut's theorem]] on mixed partial derivatives, [[Clairaut's equation]], and [[Clairaut's relation (differential geometry)|Clairaut's relation]] in differential geometry.

==Biography==

===Childhood and early life===
Clairaut was born in Paris, France, to Jean-Baptiste and Catherine Petit Clairaut. The couple had 20 children, however only a few of them survived childbirth.<ref name=":0" /> His father taught [[mathematics]]. Alexis was a [[child prodigy]]. He mastered [[Euclidean geometry]] and algebra by nine. At ten he studied [[Conic section|conic sections]] and the calculus using ''[[Analyse des infiniment petits pour l'intelligence des lignes courbes|Analyse des Infiniment Petits]]'' (1696) by  [[Guillaume de l'Hôpital]].<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=452}} At the age of twelve he wrote a memoir on four geometrical curves and under his father's tutelage he made such rapid progress in the subject that in his thirteenth year he read before the [[Académie française]] an account of the properties of four curves which he had discovered.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/the-four-curves-of-alexis-clairaut|title=The Four Curves of Alexis Clairaut|author=Taner Kiral, Jonathan Murdock and Colin B. P. McKinney|work=MAA publications|language=en-gb}}</ref> When only sixteen he finished a treatise on [[Torsion of a curve|Tortuous Curves]], ''Recherches sur les courbes a double courbure'', which, on its publication in 1731, procured his admission into the [[French Academy of Sciences|Royal Academy of Sciences]], although he was below the legal age as he was only eighteen. He gave a path-breaking formulae called the distance formulae which helps to find out the distance between any 2 points on the cartesian or XY plane.

=== Personal life and death ===
Clairaut never married and was known for leading an active social life.<ref name=":0" /> His growing popularity in society hindered his scientific work: "He was focused," says [[Charles Bossut|Bossut]], "with dining and with evenings, coupled with a lively taste for women, and seeking to make his pleasures into his day to day work, he lost rest, health, and finally life at the age of fifty-two." Though he led a fulfilling social life, he was very prominent in the advancement of learning in young mathematicians.

He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] of London on 27 October 1737.<ref>{{cite web| url= https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27clairaut%27%29| title= Fellow Details: Clairaut; Alexis Claude (1713 - 1765)| publisher= [[Royal Society]]| access-date= 2018-04-26| archive-date= 23 July 2019| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190723202724/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqCmd=Show.tcl&dsqDb=Persons&dsqPos=0&dsqSearch=%28%28text%29%3D%27clairaut%27%29| url-status= dead}}</ref>

Clairaut died in Paris in 1765. The [[Clairaut (crater)|Clairaut crater]] on the [[Moon]] was named after him in 1935.<ref name=GPN>{{gpn|1226|Clairaut|access-date=2025-03-07}}</ref>

== Contributions ==

=== Mathematics ===
In his research on the calculus, Clairaut discovered the equality of mixed partial derivatives ([[Symmetry of second derivatives|Clairaut's theorem]]).<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Itard|first=Jean|author-link=|title=[[Dictionary of Scientific Biography]]|publisher=Charles Scribner's Sons|year=1970–1980|editor-last=Gillispie|editor-first=Charles Coulston|editor-link=Charles Coulston Gillispie|location=New York|at=Alexis Clairaut}}</ref> He gave a condition under which the differential equation <math>M (x, y) \, dx + N (x, y) \,dy = 0</math> was [[Exact differential equation|exact]], namely, <math>M_y = N_x</math>.<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=452}} 

He showed that a differential equation of the form <math>y = xy' + f(y')</math>, now known as [[Clairaut's equation]], could by solved by substituting <math>p = y'</math> and differentiating both sides.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last1=Boyer |first1=Carl B. |author-link1=Carl Benjamin Boyer |title=A History of Mathematics |last2=Merzbach |first2=Uta |author-link2=Uta Merzbach |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1991 |isbn=0-471-09763-2 |edition=2nd |location=New York}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=451}} He also established the existence of the [[integrating factor]] for first-order linear differential equations. However, he had been anticipated by [[Nicolas Fatio de Duillier|Nicolas Fatio de Dullier]] in 1687, and by [[Johann Bernoulli]] in a lesson given to L’Hôpital.<ref name=":5" /> 

In 1741, Clairaut published ''Éléments de Géométrie'', aimed at beginners. For Clairaut, it was imperative for students to make discoveries themselves in a form of active, [[experiential learning]].<ref>{{Cite book
| url = https://archive.org/details/elementsgeometr00claigoog
| title = Elements of geometry, tr. by J. Kaines
| last = Clairaut
| first = Alexis Claude
| date = 1 January 1881
}}</ref> He began by comparing geometric shapes to measurements of land, a familiar topic, and covered lines, shapes, and even some three dimensional objects. Throughout the book, he copiously related geometry to other branches of mathematics as well as physics and astronomy. Some of the theories and learning methods outlined in the book are still used by teachers today, in geometry and other topics.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last = Smith
| first = David
|year = 1921
| title = Review of Èléments de Géométrie. 2 vols.
| journal = The Mathematics Teacher
}}</ref> This textbook was so popular that it went through six editions.<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=458}} In the eighteenth century, [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] extended the contributions of Clairaut and [[Christiaan Huygens]] in the geometry introducing the notion of [[Gaussian curvature]].<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=506}}

Clairaut's ''Éléments de Algèbre'' (1740) was also well-received in Continental Europe. Its sixth edition was published in 1801.<ref name=":12" />{{Reference page|page=458}}

===Figure of the Earth===
[[File:Clairaut-2.jpg|thumb|''Théorie de la Figure de la Terre, tirée des Principes de l’Hydrostatique'', 1743]]
In 1736, together with [[Pierre Louis Maupertuis]], he took part in the expedition to [[Sápmi|Lapland]], which was undertaken for the purpose of estimating a degree of the [[meridian arc]].<ref>{{cite web |last=O'Connor and |first=J. J. |author2=E. F. Robertson |title=Alexis Clairaut |work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews, Scotland |date=October 1998 |url=http://www-groups.dcs.st-and.ac.uk/~history/Biographies/Clairaut.html |access-date=12 March 2009}}</ref> The goal of the excursion was to determine the [[figure of the Earth]] and to test whether the Earth was an oblate spheroid, as Sir Isaac Newton had claimed in his book ''Principia'', or that it was an oblong, as [[Giovanni Domenico Cassini|Giovanni Cassini]] had thought.<ref name=":5" /> Before the expedition team returned to Paris, Clairaut sent his calculations to the [[Royal Society|Royal Society of London]]. The writing was later published by the society in the 1736–37 volume of ''[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society|Philosophical Transactions]].''<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Claude|first1=Alexis|last2=Colson|first2=John|year=1737|title=An Inquiry concerning the Figure of Such Planets as Revolve about an Axis, Supposing the Density Continually to Vary, from the Centre towards the Surface|jstor=103921|journal=Philosophical Transactions|volume=40|pages=277–306|doi=10.1098/rstl.1737.0045|doi-access=free}}</ref> Initially, Clairaut disagreed with Newton's conclusion. In the article, he outlines several key problems that effectively disprove Newton's calculations, and provides some solutions to the complications. The issues addressed include calculating gravitational attraction, the rotation of an ellipsoid on its axis, and the difference in density of an ellipsoid on its axes.<ref name=":1" /> At the end of his letter, Clairaut wrote: <blockquote>"It appears even Sir Isaac Newton was of the opinion, that it was necessary the Earth should be more dense toward the center, in order to be so much the flatter at the poles: and that it followed from this greater flatness, that gravity increased so much the more from the equator towards the Pole."<ref name=":1" /> </blockquote>
This meant not only that the Earth is an ellipsoid, but it is flattened more at the poles and is wider at the center, that is, an oblate spheroid. His article in ''Philosophical Transactions'' created much controversy, as he addressed the problems of Newton's theory, but provided few solutions to how to fix the calculations. 

After his return, he published his treatise ''Théorie de la figure de la terre'' (1743). In this work he promulgated a result, now known as [[Clairaut's theorem]], which connects the [[gravity]] at points on the surface of a rotating [[ellipsoid]] with the compression and the centrifugal force at the [[equator]]. His formula gave the Earth's gravitational field strength as a function of latitude.<ref name=":5" /> This hydrostatic model of the shape of the Earth was founded on a paper by the Scottish mathematician [[Colin Maclaurin]], which had shown that a mass of [[wiktionary:Homogeneous|homogeneous]] fluid set in rotation about a line through its [[center of mass]] would, under the mutual attraction of its particles, take the form of a [[Maclaurin spheroid]]. Under the assumption that the Earth was composed of concentric ellipsoidal shells of uniform density, Clairaut's theorem could be applied to it, and allowed the [[Eccentricity (mathematics)|eccentricity]] (or deviation from being a perfect sphere) of the Earth to be calculated from surface measurements of gravity. This validated Newton's calculation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite encyclopedia
| last = Knight | first = Judson |year = 2000 | title = Alexis Claude Clairaut
| url = https://archive.org/stream/B-001-002-830/Gale%20-%20Science%20and%20Its%20Times%20Vol%2004%20%281700%20to%201799%29#page/n261/mode/2up/
| encyclopedia = Science and Its Times, Vol. 4: 1700-1799 | editor1-last = Schlager | editor1-first = Neil | editor2-last = Lauer | editor2-first = Josh | pages=247–248 | access-date = 2018-04-26}}</ref> In 1849 [[Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet|George Stokes]] showed that Clairaut's result was true whatever the interior constitution or density of the Earth, provided the surface was a spheroid of equilibrium of small eccentricity.

===Mathematical astronomy===
One of the most controversial issues of the 18th century was the [[Three-body problem|problem of three bodies]], or how the Earth, Moon, and Sun are attracted to one another. With the use of the recently founded [[Leibnizian]] [[calculus]], Clairaut was able to solve the problem using four differential equations.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Bodenmann|first=Siegfried|date=January 2010|title=The 18th century battle over lunar motion|journal=Physics Today|volume=63|issue=1|pages=27–32|doi=10.1063/1.3293410|bibcode=2010PhT....63a..27B|doi-access=free}}</ref> He was also able to incorporate Newton's [[inverse-square law]] and law of attraction into his solution, with minor edits to it. However, these equations only offered approximate measurement, and no exact calculations. Another issue still remained with the three body problem; how the Moon rotates on its apsides. Even Newton could account for only half of the motion of the [[Apsis|apsides]].<ref name=":2" /> This issue had puzzled astronomers. In fact, Clairaut had at first deemed the dilemma so inexplicable, that he was on the point of publishing a new hypothesis as to the law of attraction.
[[File:Clairaut-5.jpg|thumb|''Théorie de la Lune & Tables de la Lune,'' 1765]]
The question of the apsides was a heated debate topic in Europe. Along with Clairaut, there were two other mathematicians who were racing to provide the first explanation for the three body problem; [[Leonhard Euler]] and [[Jean le Rond d'Alembert]].<ref name=":2" /> Euler and d'Alembert were arguing against the use of Newtonian laws to solve the three-body problem. Euler in particular believed that the inverse square law needed revision to accurately calculate the apsides of the Moon.

Despite the hectic competition to come up with the correct solution, Clairaut obtained an ingenious approximate solution of the problem of the three bodies. In 1750 he gained the prize of the [[Russian Academy of Science|St Petersburg Academy]] for his essay ''Théorie de la lune''; the team made up of Clairaut, [[Joseph Jérôme Lefrançois de Lalande|Jérome Lalande]] and [[Nicole-Reine Lepaute|Nicole Reine Lepaute]] successfully computed the date of the 1759 return of Halley's comet.<ref>{{cite book |first=David Alan |last=Grier |chapter=The First Anticipated Return: Halley's Comet 1758 |title=When Computers Were Human |location=Princeton |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |year=2005 |pages=11–25 |isbn=0-691-09157-9 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YTcDAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA11 }}</ref> The ''Théorie de la lune'' is strictly Newtonian in character. This contains the explanation of the motion of the [[apsis]]. It occurred to him to carry the approximation to the third order, and he thereupon found that the result was in accordance with the observations. This was followed in 1754 by some lunar tables, which he computed using a form of the [[discrete Fourier transform]].<ref>{{Cite book
|title=Fourier analysis on finite groups and applications
|first=Audrey
|last=Terras
|author-link=Audrey Terras
|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]
|date=1999
|isbn=978-0-521-45718-7
|url=https://archive.org/details/fourieranalysiso0000terr
|url-access=registration
}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=-B2TA669dJMC&pg=PA30#PPA30,M1 p. 30]</ref>

The newfound solution to the problem of three bodies ended up meaning more than proving Newton's laws correct. The unravelling of the problem of three bodies also had practical importance. It allowed sailors to determine the [[Longitude|longitudinal]] direction of their ships, which was crucial not only in sailing to a location, but finding their way home as well.<ref name=":2" /> This held economic implications as well, because sailors were able to more easily find destinations of trade based on the longitudinal measures.

In the same work, Clairaut introduced for the first time the [[Potential theory|theory of potentials]], known by that name since the [[An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism|1828 essay]] of [[George Green (mathematician)|George Green]].<ref name=":5" />

Clairaut subsequently wrote various papers on the [[orbit]] of the [[Moon]], and on the motion of [[comet]]s as affected by the perturbation of the planets, particularly on the path of [[Comet Halley|Halley's comet]]. He also used applied mathematics to study [[Venus]], taking accurate measurements of the planet's size and distance from the Earth. This was the first precise reckoning of the planet's size.

Clairaut used his own contributions to celestial mechanics and astronomy to assist [[Émilie du Châtelet]] in her translation and commentary of Newton's ''Principia''.<ref name=":5" />
